units.title: Classification, Sedation and Hypnosis
units.guide: Sedative-hypnotic drugs are classified into GABAA agonists (benzodiazepines, barbiturates and Z compounds), melatonin agonists and dual orexin receptor antagonists (DORA). Sedation means an anxiolytic/calming effect, while hypnosis means inducing sleep.

units.title: GABAA Agonists: Benzodiazepines and Barbiturates
units.sec: GABAA Agonists: Benzodiazepines and Barbiturates · p120
units.guide: GABA binds to its binding sites and opens the Cl- channel so inward Cl- movement hyperpolarises the cell and produces sedation and hypnosis; the alpha-1 subunit mediates sedation/hypnotic effects and alpha-2 other functions, while bicuculline acts as a GABA antagonist at the same site. Benzodiazepines are full agonists that increase the frequency of Cl- channel opening by GABA, are safer and can cause anterograde amnesia, whereas barbiturates increase the duration of channel opening, decrease glutamate release, act as GABA mimetics in high dose and are less safe. Phenobarbitone is DOC in neonatal seizure (commonest due to hepatic ischemic encephalopathy, acting by lowering cerebral metabolic rate) and in Crigler Najjar syndrome II (by enzyme induction), while its side effect is acute intermittent porphyria from enzyme (alpha-aminolevulinic) induction.

units.title: Metabolism of Benzodiazepines
units.guide: Benzodiazepines metabolised by plasma pseudocholinesterase are ultra short acting, and remimazolam is used for sedation in short procedures under 30 minutes. In the liver, drugs undergoing phase I + phase II glucuronidation are longest acting: diazepam (status epilepticus, muscle relaxant, febrile seizure by the rectal route), chlordiazepoxide and chlorazepate (used in alcohol dependence, chlorazepate more preferred), alprazolam (anxiolytic, used before surgery), flurazepam (insomnia, can cause nightmares) and flunitrazepam (abused in date rape because it is tasteless). Drugs with faster glucuronidation are shortest acting: triazolam and midazolam, the latter used IV for status epilepticus and anesthesia and by the buccal/intranasal route (preferred in children with acute repetitive seizures). Phase II only drugs are short acting, safe in liver failure and in the elderly (no active metabolite), remembered as LETO: lorazepam (DOC in status epilepticus), estazolam, temazepam (benzodiazepine of choice for insomnia) and oxazepam.

units.title: Dual Orexin Receptor Antagonists (DORA)
units.guide: DORA drugs inhibit both orexin receptors R1 and R2. Orexin normally acts on R1 and R2 to increase wakefulness and decrease stress. They are used for sleep induction and maintenance, their side effect is sedation so they should be avoided during the day, and the two drugs are suvorexant and daridorexant.

units.title: Melatonin Agonists
units.guide: Melatonin agonists stimulate the melatonin receptor R1 and R2 and are commonly used for sleep induction. Ramelteon is less effective than benzodiazepines/Z compounds but causes less sedation and less dependence, has only 2% oral bioavailability and is also used for jet lag. Agomelatine is used in resistant depression and tasimelteon is used in the blind for sleep/awake disorder. The sedation ranking on the page is DORA > Z compound > melatonin agonist.

units.title: Treatment of Insomnia
units.guide: In a patient complaining of insomnia, the clinician checks whether the problem is sleep induction or sleep maintenance with or without induction. If there is elderly status, decreased cognition or opioid abuse, sleep induction is treated with ramelteon and otherwise with DORA or a Z compound. For sleep maintenance with or without induction, the presence of elderly status/decreased cognition/opioid abuse leads to DORA and then doxepin if there is no response, while in their absence DORA is used first, then a Z compound and finally doxepin. Melatonin supplement can also be used to treat insomnia with the advantage of no side effects.
